name: Capsaicin
lead: Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) is the main pungent compound in chili peppers. It and related capsaicinoids are produced by plants of the genus Capsicum, likely as a deterrent to mammals and fungi, and it causes a burning sensation on contact with tissues in mammals [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles capsaicin is used for a body-composition goal: a leaner, more defined physique. Chili peppers, hot sauces and capsaicin or red-pepper-extract capsules are added to diets and to thermogenic fat-burner products on the premise that they raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation or reduce appetite, helping someone reach a lower body-fat level and so show more muscle and a sharper jawline and face [1][5][6]. Topical capsaicin creams are also used for joint and muscle aches, which can matter for people who train hard [1][27].

As a prescription topical, a high-concentration (8%) patch (Qutenza) was approved by the US FDA and in the European Union in 2009 for pain from post-herpetic neuralgia and has since been studied in diabetic neuropathy [1][8]. Research on capsaicin as a weight-management aid includes a 2023 meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials and several small controlled studies of energy expenditure and fat oxidation [5][6][7].
Capsaicin acts by binding the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing neurons, work that contributed to the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian [1][22].

chain: Eaten as chili or taken as a supplement
Small rise in heat production and fat oxidation, and in some studies a lower appetite
Slightly easier calorie deficit, so a leaner physique over time
angle.text: Capsaicin is used as a small add-on to a fat-loss diet. Studies measure modest changes in energy expenditure, fat oxidation, body weight and waist size, and the effect on appearance runs through the overall calorie deficit and training.

paras: Capsaicin is added to thermogenic fat-burner supplements and eaten in chilis in the belief that it increases heat production, fat oxidation and satiety [1]. Wikipedia's thermogenics article describes bodybuilders using such products to try to raise basal metabolic rate and reduce body fat, with caffeine and ephedrine the best-known components of classic stacks [28]. Researchers have measured capsaicin's effects under controlled conditions, including acute energy expenditure and fat oxidation and substrate oxidation after modest weight loss [5][6][7].

On T Nation's forum members describe capsaicin as one ingredient among several in cutting-phase routines. One long-running training log lists capsaicin alongside other supplements in a fat-loss stack [24], and a 2008 thread by a poster said he had been experimenting with red pepper extract and considered it a reasonable thing to add to a fat-loss phase, particularly in the later stages [23]. Another poster said spicy food helped with leg cramps while using clenbuterol [26].

Topical capsaicin relieves some neuropathic pain by desensitising nociceptor fibres. A 2017 review described moderate to substantial relief of post-herpetic, HIV and diabetic neuropathic pain with the 8% preparation versus a 0.4% control, with limited quality of evidence, and the 12-week phase III trial in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy found a larger pain reduction with the 8% patch than placebo (about 27 percent versus 21 percent) [1][8]. Reviews of neuropathic pain treatment and of painful diabetic neuropathy discuss capsaicin among the options [9][10][11]. Wikipedia notes insufficient evidence for itch (pruritus) and low-quality evidence that oral capsaicin may modestly lower LDL cholesterol [1].

Over-the-counter capsaicin creams carry labelling for temporary relief of minor aches and pains of muscles and joints from backache, arthritis, strains and sprains. Labels advise external use only, testing on a small area first, avoiding eyes, lips and mucous membranes, not using on wounds or damaged skin, and not applying heat to the treated area; they warn that a burning sensation is expected and generally fades with regular use [27]. A lifter on T Nation reported applying capsaicin cream to a sore elbow and said it helped [25].

Capsaicin gives the heat in chili powder, hot sauces and curries, and capsaicinoids are the active ingredients in pepper sprays and in repellents for mammals such as deer and rabbits [1][21]. Law-enforcement sprays are often rated at 500,000 to 2,000,000 Scoville heat units, a measure Wikipedia calls unreliable for sprays [21]. Capsaicin is banned in equestrian sports, and four horses were disqualified after testing positive at the 2008 Olympic show jumping events [1].

sections.h: Effectiveness for weight and body composition
paras: A 2023 British Journal of Nutrition meta-analysis pooled 15 randomised trials with 762 overweight or obese adults. Capsaicin supplementation was associated with a small reduction in body weight (about 0.5 kg), BMI (about 0.25 kg/m2) and waist circumference (about 1.1 cm), with no significant change in waist-to-hip ratio; the authors described the effects as fairly small and called for more prospective studies [5].

A 2013 PLOS ONE study used a single-blind crossover design in which 15 healthy adults spent four 36-hour stays in a respiration chamber, eating either full or reduced energy with or without capsaicin (about 2.56 mg per meal from red chili). In the reduced-energy condition, capsaicin was associated with higher fat oxidation and with the avoidance of the drop in some energy expenditure measures seen with calorie restriction alone; blood pressure did not differ significantly. The study was funded by a spice company and the authors noted the small sample [6]. An earlier trial examined substrate oxidation and weight maintenance after modest weight loss [7].

Wikipedia reports that, as of 2007, no evidence had shown weight loss to be directly correlated with ingesting capsaicin; that well-designed research has been hampered because the pungency of the doses used prevented participants from complying; and that a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that taking it before a meal might slightly reduce food intake and shift preference toward carbohydrates [1].

Christian Friedrich Bucholz first extracted it in impure form in 1816, and Rudolf Buchheim (1873) and Endre Hogyes (1878) attributed the burning feeling to the substance [1]. Wikipedia adds that J. C. Thresh obtained it in almost pure form in the 1870s and that its structure and synthesis were worked out in the 1910s and 1930s [1]. The first pesticide registered by the US Department of Agriculture containing only capsaicin was approved in 1962 [1].

Pure capsaicin is a hydrophobic, crystalline white solid that dissolves well in alcohol and poorly in water. The common capsaicinoids are capsaicin (about 69 percent of the mix), dihydrocapsaicin (about 22 percent) and nordihydrocapsaicin (about 7 percent) [1]. Pungency is measured in Scoville heat units; capsaicin itself rates about 16,000,000 [1]. It is concentrated in the placental tissue that holds the seeds. Birds lack a sensitive capsaicin receptor and disperse the seeds, which fits the idea that the compound deters mammals [1]. Capsinoids are related non-pungent compounds found in paprika [1].

Capsaicin binds the TRPV1 ion channel on nociceptors, which is also activated by heat above about 43 degrees C and by acid, causing cation influx, depolarisation and sensations of burning. Prolonged activation leads to desensitisation or defunctionalisation of the fibres, which underlies its use as an analgesic [1][3][4][19][22]. TRPV1 was cloned in 1997 by David Julius's group as a heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway, and mice lacking it showed impaired pain sensation [18][20][22]. Wikipedia notes that TRPV1 also appears to help regulate body temperature: antagonists of the channel often raise body temperature, and one was dropped from clinical trials because of hyperthermia [22].

Oral capsaicin is efficiently absorbed from the gut (85 percent in rats) but undergoes extensive first-pass liver metabolism. In human volunteers who ingested a Capsicum extract, the blood half-life was about 25 minutes with peak levels at 45 minutes. Topical capsaicin reaches the stratum corneum within a minute [1].

Capsaicin is a strong irritant of skin, eyes and airways. Ingesting large amounts can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and burning diarrhea, and eye exposure causes intense tearing and pain; Wikipedia also reports that ingestion of very high quantities can be fatal, particularly in people with heart problems, and that myocardial infarction has been reported after ingesting capsaicin capsules [1]. The reported LD50 in mice is 47.2 mg/kg [1]. Pepper exposures are among the most common plant-related calls to poison centres [1]. Plain water is ineffective at removing it from skin; alcohol dissolves it, and cold milk may relieve burning after ingestion [1]. Wikipedia's pepper spray article reports that eye irritation from sprays can persist for up to 24 hours and that deaths have been linked to police use of sprays, with causes debated [21].

Capsaicin is legal and unscheduled as a food ingredient and supplement. The 8% Qutenza patch is prescription-only in the United States, approved by the FDA in 2009 and authorised in the European Union [1]. Civilian pepper spray is banned in the UK, Mexico and Hong Kong, restricted in many European countries and legal with limits in all 50 US states [21].

For weight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials examined capsaicin intake in overweight and obese subjects, a PLOS ONE study measured the acute effects of capsaicin on energy expenditure and fat oxidation, and an earlier trial examined substrate oxidation and weight maintenance after modest weight loss [5][6][7]. For pain: the 8% patch trial enrolled 369 patients, with a shorter median time to response (19 versus 72 days) and modest improvements in sleep interference; application-site reactions were the main adverse events [8]. Other registered trials examine the patch in cancer-related neuropathic pain, post-surgical neuropathic pain, coccygodynia and amputation [12][13][14]. A 2024 randomized trial tested topical capsaicin for delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and a 2015 trial tested its use in cough reduction [15][16]. Reviews of burning mouth syndrome treatment also include capsaicin [17].

timeline.event: Capsaicin first extracted in impure form by Christian Friedrich Bucholz [1].
Rudolf Buchheim attributes the burning sensation to the extract [1].
Endre Hogyes also attributes the burning sensation to it [1].
First USDA-registered pesticide using only capsaicin approved [1].
The capsaicin receptor (TRPV1) cloned as a heat-activated ion channel [18][22].
Four horses disqualified for capsaicin at the Olympic show jumping events [1].
Capsaicin 8% patch approved by FDA and EU for post-herpetic neuralgia pain [1].
PLOS ONE respiration-chamber crossover study of capsaicin and fat oxidation [6].
Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognises discovery of temperature and touch receptors, including work using capsaicin [1][22].
Meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials of capsaicin in overweight and obese adults published [5].

lore.intro: On bodybuilding forums capsaicin appears mainly as a small cutting-phase add-on in diet and supplement stacks, and as a topical for sore joints [23][24][25].

claims.claim: Hot peppers or capsaicin capsules speed up fat loss.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said he considered red pepper extract a good thing to add to a fat-loss phase, especially in the later stages [23]; a member's log lists capsaicin in a fat-loss supplement stack [24].
claims.experts: A 2023 meta-analysis of 15 trials found small average reductions in weight, BMI and waist circumference; Wikipedia reports that compliance with high pungent doses has hampered research [1][5].

claims.claim: Capsaicin boosts metabolism and fat oxidation.
claims.believers: Supplement makers and forum posters describe it as a thermogenic that burns extra calories.
claims.experts: A respiration-chamber crossover study of 15 adults reported higher fat oxidation and preserved energy expenditure during calorie restriction with capsaicin, in a small company-funded study [6]; an earlier trial examined substrate oxidation after modest weight loss [7].

claims.believers: Users describe feeling fuller or eating less on spicy meals.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that taking it before a meal might slightly reduce food intake [1].

claims.claim: Capsaicin cream helps sore joints and tendons for lifters.
claims.believers: A lifter in a T Nation log said applying capsaicin to his elbow helped [25].
claims.experts: Over-the-counter labels list temporary relief of minor aches and pains of muscles and joints; the 8% prescription patch has been studied in neuropathic pain [8][27].

claims.claim: Spicy food helps with cramps during a cut.
claims.believers: A T Nation member said spicy food helped his leg cramps while using clenbuterol [26].
claims.experts: No published study has tested capsaicin for cramps related to clenbuterol use.

claims.claim: Capsaicin is harmless because it is just food.
claims.believers: Forum members eat very hot peppers regularly as a normal addition to meals.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports nausea, vomiting and burning diarrhea with large amounts, and rare reports of myocardial infarction after capsaicin capsules; it is a strong irritant of skin, eyes and airways [1].
